archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-five defense is good enough to beat anyone, attached to a below-average, run-leaning offense whose turnovers and backup-quarterback play keep the record near .500.

report.headline: Elite defense, giveaway-prone offense: a better team than 5-4, not a finished one
report.take:
Seattle is still Mike Macdonald's defense first. Last year's 14-3 team led the league in EPA allowed, and this one is fifth, second in success rate allowed and first in yards allowed per game. What separates it is what it refuses to give up: no defense allows explosive passes less often, and none is better against the deep ball. Opponents convert only 30.6% of third downs. Most weeks this unit keeps games within reach on its own.

The record is 5-4 instead of better because of the other side of the ball. The offense ranks 23rd in EPA, and the split explains why. The passing game is roughly league average (14th in pass EPA), but the run game is 28th and still gets called more than the situation suggests, with a pass rate over expected that ranks 27th. The line allows pressure more often than any in the league. The bigger problem is giveaways: 14 turnovers and a turnover differential that ranks 26th. Every loss Drew Lock has started came with at least three giveaways, including four against San Francisco. With Sam Darnold hurt, Lock has made six of the nine starts. When he protects the ball, as in the clean 17-3 win over Arizona, this team rarely loses.

The numbers hide a little bad luck. The point differential implies 5.9 wins against the actual five, and wins over expected sits at -0.94 after last year's +3.29. Some regression went against them, and there is some coming back. The one defensive flaw is real, though: once opponents reach the red zone they score touchdowns 75% of the time, 29th in the league. That bend-don't-break math only holds if the offense isn't handing over short fields.

Where this goes depends on health and ball security more than talent. Darnold's return estimate falls around the San Francisco trip. Both starting tackles-and-guards anchors, Charles Cross and Quenton Nelson, are out this week on a line that was already the most pressured in football. The defense makes a wild-card floor realistic. The offense decides whether there is anything above it.

strengths.title: Nothing gets behind this secondary
strengths.body: Seattle ranks first in explosive pass rate allowed and first in deep-pass EPA allowed. Opponents have to string together long drives against a defense that is second in success rate allowed. This is a schematic identity carried over from last year's top-ranked unit, not a hot streak, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Pressure that finishes drives
strengths.body: The front ranks fifth in pressure rate and third in QB hit rate. That shows up on the money down, where Seattle allows third-down conversions only 30.6% of the time. With Leonard Williams and Uchenna Nwosu out this week the rush gets thinner, but depth has carried it so far.

strengths.title: Hidden yards on special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add value most weeks, ranking fifth in EPA per game. For a team whose offense struggles to sustain drives, field position from the kicking game quietly matters. Special-teams play is noisier than offense or defense, but it has been a consistent plus.

concerns.title: Turnovers are the whole story
concerns.body: Fourteen giveaways and a turnover differential ranked 26th have turned an elite defense into a .500 team. The worst outbreaks came in Lock's starts against Washington, San Francisco and Denver, all losses. Some of this is quarterback play and some is a line under constant pressure. Neither fix is coming immediately.

concerns.title: A losing run game they keep calling
concerns.body: The run game ranks 28th in EPA. The line is 32nd in pressure rate allowed and 27th in short-yardage conversion, yet Seattle passes less than expected. That is a choice to protect the quarterback and the defense, but it caps the offense. It gets harder this week without Cross and Nelson, who both played nearly every snap.

concerns.title: Red-zone leak behind the wall
concerns.body: Opponents who reach the red zone score touchdowns 75% of the time, 29th in the league. Short passing is also only 21st in EPA allowed. Teams that are patient underneath can still finish drives, especially after a turnover hands them a short field.

trend.note: Results have swung with ball security more than opponent quality. Clean games against New England, Kansas City and Arizona became wins, while multi-turnover games against Washington, San Francisco and Denver became one-score losses. The Week 8 blowout loss to Chicago was the one game the defense itself broke.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Raiders defense, but its pass rush meets a patched line
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas is the inverse of Seattle: a functional offense attached to a defense that is last in points allowed and 31st in success rate allowed. The Raiders are worst in the league against short passes and 31st in explosive run rate allowed. Kirk Cousins has started every game and runs a passing attack that ranks 10th in EPA with the league's second-lowest sack rate. The Raiders can't run, though, 30th in rush EPA and last in yards per carry, so Seattle's defense can focus on Cousins. The Book has Seattle -3.5 with a 43.5 total, and Las Vegas has covered two-thirds of its games.

Availability tilts the matchup toward the Raiders' one defensive strength. Seattle is without left-side anchors Charles Cross and Quenton Nelson against a pass rush ranked third in pressure rate and fourth in takeaways. Darnold is out, and Lock is questionable with an oblique strain that his coach expects him to play through. On defense, Leonard Williams, Uchenna Nwosu and Brandon Pili are all listed out, which thins the front. Seattle's WR3 Rashid Shaheed is also out. The Raiders are missing rotational DT Thomas Booker IV, and backup center Trey Zuhn III is in concussion protocol.

waysToWin.title: Quick game into a soft underbelly
waysToWin.body: The Raiders allow the most EPA in the league on short passes, and their WR2 coverage has been the worst in football. Getting the ball out fast to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp and AJ Barner beats the pressure and the matchup at the same time. It also keeps Lock out of the long-developing throws that produced his turnovers.

waysToWin.title: Make Cousins drive the length of the field
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas has no ground game to lean on, and Seattle takes away the deep shot better than anyone. That leaves the Raiders needing 10-play drives against a defense that stops third downs. If the red-zone defense holds even once or twice, the Raiders' path to 20-plus points narrows sharply.

waysToWin.title: Lead back against a weak run fit
waysToWin.body: Opposing lead backs have scored well above their norm against Las Vegas, which also gives up explosive runs at the second-highest rate in the league. Even a below-average Seattle run game can pick up chunk yards here and protect a lead late.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush meets missing tackles
waysToLose.body: Seattle's line was already the league's most pressured, and now it is without its two most-used starters. The Raiders' rush ranks third in pressure rate. Strip-sacks and hurried throws are exactly how Lock's bad games have unfolded.

waysToLose.title: Another three-giveaway day
waysToLose.body: Las Vegas ranks fourth in takeaways, and Seattle ranks 26th in turnover differential. Short fields expose the defense's one weak spot in the red zone and erase the yardage edge. That is how Seattle lost to Washington and Denver despite outplaying both between the 20s.

waysToLose.title: Cousins picks apart the middle
waysToLose.body: Cousins rarely takes sacks and runs a top-10 passing offense that targets tight ends well above the league share. Seattle is only 21st against short passes and is missing two front-seven regulars. A patient, chain-moving Raiders offense could keep the game close enough for one mistake to decide it.

nextGame.watch: How Seattle protects Lock on early downs without Cross and Nelson. Quick throws and a clean turnover sheet make this a comfortable road win; a couple of strip-sacks make it a coin flip.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the sustainable part. It was the league's best a year ago and is top five again in nearly every efficiency measure, so expect it to keep holding opponents under 20 most weeks. The turnover rate is the part most likely to move. Some of it is Lock and will ease if Darnold returns around the San Francisco trip, and the point differential already says this team has been unlucky by about a win. The offense's ceiling stays limited as long as the line is beat up and the run game ranks near the bottom, so the offense needs to shrink its mistakes rather than expect a surge.

The schedule splits cleanly. Dallas, Philadelphia and Carolina bring defenses that can be attacked, while two games against the Rams' fourth-ranked defense and a trip to 7-1 San Francisco will test a thin offense. Seattle sits behind the 49ers in the division, so the realistic target is a wild card. Getting there likely comes down to the two Rams games and avoiding a giveaway-driven loss to a team it should beat.
swingFactors: Darnold's return and health at quarterback
Cross and Nelson back in the lineup
The two late games against the Rams

confidence.note: Defensive profile is stable year over year; offense hinges on QB and line injuries over nine games.
